claim: Topographic representation of the receptor surface is a fundamental feature of sensory cortical organization.
source: Topographic representation of the receptor surface is a fundamental feature of sensory cortical organization.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about sensory cortical organization.

claim: Topographic representation is imparted by the thalamus, which relays information from the periphery to the cortex.
source: This is imparted by the thalamus, which relays information from the periphery to the cortex.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about thalamic function.

claim: The frequency selectivity of individual thalamocortical axons is surprisingly heterogeneous, even in layers 3b/4 of the primary cortical areas.
source: we found that the frequency selectivity of individual thalamocortical axons is surprisingly heterogeneous, even in layers 3b/4 of the primary cortical areas, where the thalamic input is dominated by the lemniscal projection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the two-photon calcium imaging data presented in the study.

claim: Thalamic input to layers 3b/4 is dominated by the lemniscal projection.
source: even in layers 3b/4 of the primary cortical areas, where the thalamic input is dominated by the lemniscal projection.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical experiments and established knowledge about auditory thalamocortical projections.

claim: Thalamocortical input to layer 1 includes collaterals from axons innervating layers 3b/4.
source: We also show that thalamocortical input to layer 1 includes collaterals from axons innervating layers 3b/4 and is largely in register with the main input targeting those layers.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical observations showing axons traveling from middle layers to L1.

claim: Thalamocortical input to layer 1 is largely in register with the main input targeting layers 3b/4.
source: We also show that thalamocortical input to layer 1 includes collaterals from axons innervating layers 3b/4 and is largely in register with the main input targeting those layers.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation between mean BF of L1 and L3b/4 regions shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Locally varied thalamocortical projections may be useful in enabling rapid contextual modulation of cortical frequency representations.
source: Such locally varied thalamocortical projections may be useful in enabling rapid contextual modulation of cortical frequency representations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed heterogeneity.

claim: The vast majority of ascending sensory information reaches the cortex via the thalamus.
source: The vast majority of ascending sensory information reaches the cortex via the thalamus.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about sensory pathways.

claim: Most of the brain's auditory neurons are tuned to sound frequency.
source: Most of the brain's auditory neurons, including those in the medial geniculate body (MGB) of the thalamus, are tuned to sound frequency
evidence: This is established knowledge about auditory system organization.

claim: The spatial arrangement of auditory neurons reflects the tonotopic organization established by the biomechanical properties of the cochlea.
source: Most of the brain's auditory neurons, including those in the medial geniculate body (MGB) of the thalamus, are tuned to sound frequency and their spatial arrangement reflects the tonotopic organization established by the biomechanical properties of the cochlea.
evidence: This is established knowledge about auditory system organization.

claim: Tonotopy is preserved across species and at every lemniscal stage of the ascending auditory pathway up to the cortex.
source: Tonotopy is preserved across species and at every lemniscal stage of the ascending auditory pathway up to the cortex (Kaas, 2011; Schreiner and Winer, 2007; Woolsey and Walzl, 1942).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The presence of sound frequency gradients within brain regions is the most well characterized feature of the auditory system.
source: the presence of sound frequency gradients within each of these brain regions is therefore the most well characterized feature of the auditory system.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: How precise cortical tonotopic organization is has recently been debated.
source: While the existence of cortical tonotopy is universally accepted, how precise this organization really is has recently been debated (Guo et al., 2012; Kanold et al., 2014; Rothschild and Mizrahi, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Single-cell resolution imaging in mouse auditory cortex has questioned the smooth tonotopic organization revealed with microelectrode recordings.
source: In particular, the opportunity to image the activity of large populations of neurons at single-cell resolution in the mouse auditory cortex (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010; Issa et al., 2014; Rothschild et al., 2010; Winkowski and Kanold, 2013) has questioned the smooth tonotopic organization revealed with microelectrode recordings (Guo et al., 2012; Hackett, 2011; Stiebler et al., 1997) or low-resolution imaging methods (Horie et al., 2013; Moczulska et al., 2013; Tsukano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neurons in the main thalamorecipient layers 4 and 3b exhibit precise tonotopy that transitions into a coarse and more heterogeneous frequency organization in the supragranular layers.
source: The current view holds that neurons in the main thalamorecipient layers 4 and 3b, which tend to be most commonly sampled by microelectrode recordings, exhibit precise tonotopy that transitions into a coarse and more heterogeneous frequency organization in the supragranular layers (Kanold et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Retrograde tracing of thalamocortical inputs suggests strict topography.
source: Although retrograde tracing of thalamocortical inputs (Brandner and Redies, 1990; Hackett et al., 2011) suggests strict topography
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Anterograde tracing indicates considerable divergence in the auditory thalamocortical pathway.
source: anterograde tracing (Huang and Winer, 2000) and reconstruction of single thalamic axons (Cetas et al., 1999) indicate considerable divergence in the auditory thalamocortical pathway.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The frequency tuning of thalamic inputs that converge onto individual auditory cortical neurons can span several octaves.
source: Indeed the frequency tuning of thalamic inputs that converge onto individual auditory cortical neurons can span several octaves (Liu et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Most thalamocortical projections target the middle cortical layers.
source: Furthermore, while most thalamocortical projections target the middle cortical layers, axons from the MGB can also be found in other layers (Frost and Caviness, 1980; Huang and Winer, 2000; Ji et al., 2016; Kimura et al., 2003; Llano and Sherman, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Axons from the MGB can be found in cortical layers other than the middle layers.
source: Furthermore, while most thalamocortical projections target the middle cortical layers, axons from the MGB can also be found in other layers (Frost and Caviness, 1980; Huang and Winer, 2000; Ji et al., 2016; Kimura et al., 2003; Llano and Sherman, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nothing is currently known about the relative specificity or precision of thalamic inputs to cortical layers other than the middle layers.
source: but nothing is currently known about the relative specificity or precision of these inputs.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The study employed in vivo two-photon axonal calcium imaging to measure the frequency selectivity of individual boutons on auditory thalamocortical axons.
source: In this study, we employed in vivo two-photon (Denk et al., 1990) axonal calcium imaging (Glickfeld et al., 2013; Petreanu et al., 2012; Roth et al., 2016) to measure for the first time the frequency selectivity of individual boutons on auditory thalamocortical axons.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The tuning of neighboring boutons is surprisingly heterogeneous across different anesthetic states and different strains of mice.
source: Across different anesthetic states and different strains of mice, we found that the tuning of neighboring boutons is surprisingly heterogeneous
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Frequency gradients are apparent at a large spatial scale only.
source: that frequency gradients are apparent at a large spatial scale only
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Thalamic inputs to cortical layers 1 and 3b/4 share a similarly coarse tonotopic organization.
source: and that thalamic inputs to cortical layers 1 and 3b/4 share a similarly coarse tonotopic organization.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The organization of thalamic input reflects almost exclusively the properties of the lemniscal thalamocortical projection originating in the ventral division of the medial geniculate body.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that this organization, which provides a potential basis for the broad spectral integration and experience-dependent plasticity that are characteristic features of the tuning properties of auditory cortical neurons, reflects almost exclusively the properties of the lemniscal thalamocortical projection originating in the ventral division of the medial geniculate body.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical experiments presented in the study.

claim: The organization of thalamic input provides a potential basis for the broad spectral integration that is a characteristic feature of auditory cortical neurons.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that this organization, which provides a potential basis for the broad spectral integration and experience-dependent plasticity that are characteristic features of the tuning properties of auditory cortical neurons
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed organization.

claim: The organization of thalamic input provides a potential basis for the experience-dependent plasticity that is a characteristic feature of auditory cortical neurons.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that this organization, which provides a potential basis for the broad spectral integration and experience-dependent plasticity that are characteristic features of the tuning properties of auditory cortical neurons
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed organization.

claim: GCaMP6m was expressed throughout the auditory thalamus.
source: We initially expressed GCaMP6m (Chen et al., 2013) throughout the auditory thalamus (Figure 1A)
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Most of the thalamic axons were found in the middle layers, L3b/4.
source: Most of the thalamic axons were found in the middle layers, L3b/4, but substantial input was also observed in L1.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Substantial thalamic input was observed in L1.
source: Most of the thalamic axons were found in the middle layers, L3b/4, but substantial input was also observed in L1.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging experiments.

claim: Calcium transients in individual putative synaptic boutons correlate with somatic spiking activity.
source: We measured calcium transients, which correlate with somatic spiking activity (Petreanu et al., 2012), in individual putative synaptic boutons of thalamocortical axons (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Level-averaged tuning curves could generally be well approximated by a Gaussian.
source: Level-averaged tuning curves could generally be well approximated by a Gaussian (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For each 90 × 100 µm region of auditory cortex, dozens to hundreds of tone-responsive boutons were recorded.
source: For each 90 × 100 µm region of auditory cortex we recorded from dozens to hundreds of tone-responsive (L1: 90.5 ± 64 (median ± interquartile range), n = 36 imaged regions; L3b/4: 87 ± 84, n = 36) and mostly well-tuned boutons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the experimental data.

claim: In L1, 90.5 ± 64 (median ± interquartile range) tone-responsive boutons were recorded per region (n = 36 imaged regions).
source: For each 90 × 100 µm region of auditory cortex we recorded from dozens to hundreds of tone-responsive (L1: 90.5 ± 64 (median ± interquartile range), n = 36 imaged regions; L3b/4: 87 ± 84, n = 36)
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the experimental data.

claim: In L3b/4, 87 ± 84 tone-responsive boutons were recorded per region (n = 36 imaged regions).
source: For each 90 × 100 µm region of auditory cortex we recorded from dozens to hundreds of tone-responsive (L1: 90.5 ± 64 (median ± interquartile range), n = 36 imaged regions; L3b/4: 87 ± 84, n = 36)
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the experimental data.

claim: Even neighboring boutons could be tuned to frequencies several octaves apart both in L1 and L3b/4.
source: To our surprise, even neighboring boutons could be tuned to frequencies several octaves apart both in L1 and L3b/4 (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1D-G.

claim: The average co-tuning of thalamic boutons in a 90 × 100 µm region of auditory cortex was about one octave.
source: While the average co-tuning of thalamic boutons in a 90 × 100 µm region of auditory cortex was about one octave, there was a slight, but statistically significant, difference between the inputs to the different layers.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the experimental data.

claim: Input to L3b/4 shows stronger co-tuning (0.93 ± 0.25 octaves) than input to L1 (1.15 ± 0.37 octaves).
source: Input to L3b/4 shows stronger co-tuning (0.93 ± 0.25 octaves) and is, thus, more homogeneous than the input to L1 (1.15 ± 0.37 octaves, p<0.001, effect size: r = 0.43, n = 36, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Within L3b/4 there was no relationship between depth and co-tuning.
source: Within L3b/4 there was no relationship between depth and co-tuning (R = 0.14, p=0.41, n = 36, Spearman's correlation)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Layer 4 is no more homogeneous than lower layer 3.
source: which suggests that layer 4 is no more homogeneous than lower layer 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of relationship between depth and co-tuning within L3b/4.

claim: Mice are sensitive to frequencies between about 1 and 100 kHz.
source: Mice are sensitive to frequencies between about 1 and 100 kHz (Willott, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Most auditory nerve fibers are tuned to frequencies in the middle one to two octaves of the mouse's hearing range.
source: Most auditory nerve fibers (Ehret, 1979) and most neurons in the inferior colliculus (Stiebler and Ehret, 1985) and thalamus (Anderson and Linden, 2011) are tuned to frequencies in the middle one to two octaves of the mouse's hearing range.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most neurons in the inferior colliculus are tuned to frequencies in the middle one to two octaves of the mouse's hearing range.
source: Most auditory nerve fibers (Ehret, 1979) and most neurons in the inferior colliculus (Stiebler and Ehret, 1985) and thalamus (Anderson and Linden, 2011) are tuned to frequencies in the middle one to two octaves of the mouse's hearing range.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most neurons in the thalamus are tuned to frequencies in the middle one to two octaves of the mouse's hearing range.
source: Most auditory nerve fibers (Ehret, 1979) and most neurons in the inferior colliculus (Stiebler and Ehret, 1985) and thalamus (Anderson and Linden, 2011) are tuned to frequencies in the middle one to two octaves of the mouse's hearing range.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The overall BF distribution of thalamocortical inputs had a pronounced bias towards frequencies near the center of the mouse's hearing range.
source: Consistent with the frequency distributions reported in the inferior colliculus and thalamus, we found that the overall BF distribution of thalamocortical inputs had a pronounced bias towards frequencies near the center of the mouse's hearing range (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1H,I.

claim: The overall BF distributions for L1 (1.29 octaves) and L3b/4 (1.05 octaves) exhibited slightly but significantly weaker co-tuning than individual imaged regions.
source: We found that the overall BF distributions for L1 (1.29 octaves) and L3b/4 (1.05 octaves) exhibited slightly but significantly weaker co-tuning than individual imaged regions (L1: p=0.003, effect size: r = 0.50, n = 36; L3b/4: p=0.014, effect size: r = 0.42, n = 36, Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There is a relationship between topographic distance and the difference in BF in L3b/4.
source: Indeed, we observed a relationship between topographic distance and the difference in BF (Figure 2A). Interestingly, this very small but statistically significant correlation was present not only in the main thalamic input to L3b/4 (R = 0.034, p<10−45, for all possible pairs of boutons, n = 167521, Spearman's correlation)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a relationship between topographic distance and the difference in BF in L1.
source: Indeed, we observed a relationship between topographic distance and the difference in BF (Figure 2A). Interestingly, this very small but statistically significant correlation was present not only in the main thalamic input to L3b/4 (R = 0.034, p<10−45, for all possible pairs of boutons, n = 167521, Spearman's correlation), but also in L1 (R = 0.035, p<10−63, n = 237107, Spearman's correlation)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The relationship between distance and frequency selectivity was not simply the result of a topographic clustering of boutons from the same axon.
source: The relationship between distance and frequency selectivity was not simply the result of a topographic clustering of boutons from the same axon because the correlation remained even when pairs with the same BF were excluded from the analysis (L3b/4: R = 0.027, p<10−24, n = 142108; L1: R = 0.024, p<10−28, n = 210001, Spearman's correlation).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There is a close correspondence between the mean BF of a region imaged in L3b/4 and the mean BF of one imaged in L1 immediately above.
source: We found that there is a close correspondence between the mean BF of a region imaged in L3b/4 and the mean BF of one imaged in L1 immediately above, suggesting that the two input channels are matched tonotopically (Figure 2B, R = 0.59, p=0.0002, n = 36, Pearson correlation).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The caudo-rostral low-to-high tonotopic gradient indicative of mouse A1 emerged both in the inputs to L3b/4 and the inputs to L1 when examining several regions close together.
source: Figure 2C illustrates the results from an experiment in which gaps in the vasculature allowed us to image several regions close together. The caudo-rostral low-to-high tonotopic gradient indicative of mouse A1 now emerged both in the inputs to L3b/4 and the inputs to L1.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: C57BL/6 mice are not normally considered to suffer from impaired hearing at the age used in the study.
source: C57BL/6 mice are not normally considered to suffer from impaired hearing at the age used here (Ison et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A decline in the number of neurons tuned to high frequencies can be detected in C57BL/6 mice as early as 1–2 months after birth, especially at higher levels of the auditory pathway such as the cortex.
source: but there have been some reports that a decline in the number of neurons tuned to high frequencies can be detected as early as 1–2 months after birth, especially at higher levels of the auditory pathway such as the cortex (Willott et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The C57BL/6NTac.Cdh23753A>G strain has the Cdh23ahl allele that predisposes C57BL/6 to age-related high frequency hearing loss corrected.
source: We therefore carried out additional experiments on a novel C57BL/6 strain in which the Cdh23ahl allele that otherwise predisposes this strain to age-related high frequency hearing loss has been corrected (Mianné et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The proportion of high frequency BFs was greater in C57BL/6NTac.Cdh23753A>G mice than in C57BL/6 mice.
source: While the C57BL/6NTac.Cdh23753A>G mice also showed a bias for frequencies near the middle of their hearing range, the proportion of high frequency BFs was greater than in the C57BL/6 mice and the overall BF distribution, thus, broader (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The median number of tone-responsive boutons obtained per imaging region in awake C57BL/6NTac.Cdh23753A>G mice was 29.5 ± 23.
source: Overall, the median number of tone-responsive boutons obtained per imaging region was lower (29.5 ± 23)
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the experimental data.

claim: The average co-tuning per imaged region of auditory cortex in awake C57BL/6NTac.Cdh23753A>G mice was just above one octave both near the cortical surface and in the middle layers.
source: the results were remarkably similar. Thus, the average co-tuning per imaged region of auditory cortex was just above one octave both near the cortical surface and in the middle layers (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In awake C57BL/6NTac.Cdh23753A>G mice, co-tuning in L3b/4 (1.21 ± 0.64 octaves) was slightly stronger than in L1 (1.42 ± 0.50 octaves).
source: with slightly stronger co-tuning in L3b/4 (1.21 ± 0.64 octaves) than in L1 (1.42 ± 0.50 octaves, p=0.011, effect size: r = 0.40, n = 20, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In awake C57BL/6NTac.Cdh23753A>G mice, the inputs to L1 and L3b/4 were matched tonotopically.
source: Moreover, as in the preceding experiments, the inputs to L1 and L3b/4 were matched tonotopically (Figure 3E, R = 0.67, p=0.0013, n = 20, Pearson correlation).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The caudo-rostral, low-to-high and high-to-low tonotopic gradients that are respectively indicative of A1 and AAF emerged when imaging several regions over a large enough area in awake C57BL/6NTac.Cdh23753A>G mice.
source: Where it was possible to image several regions over a large enough area, the caudo-rostral, low-to-high and high-to-low tonotopic gradients that are respectively indicative of A1 and the anterior auditory field (AAF), the primary cortical areas of the mouse, emerged (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The vast majority (18/20) of imaging regions in awake C57BL/6NTac.Cdh23753A>G mice were located in the primary cortical areas.
source: These recordings demonstrated that the vast majority (18/20) of imaging regions were located in the primary cortical areas.
evidence: This is supported by the microelectrode recordings shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The auditory thalamus consists of several subnuclei including MGBv, MGBd, MGBm, PIN, SG, and PP.
source: The auditory thalamus consists of several subnuclei. Besides the ventral division of the MGB (MGBv), which is the largest subnucleus and part of the lemniscal pathway, these are the non-lemniscal dorsal division of the MGB (MGBd) and the paralaminar nuclei —the medial division of the MGB (MGBm), the posterior intralaminar nucleus (PIN), the suprageniculate nucleus (SG) and peripeduncular nucleus (PP).
evidence: This is established knowledge about auditory thalamus anatomy.

claim: MGBv is the largest subnucleus of the auditory thalamus and part of the lemniscal pathway.
source: Besides the ventral division of the MGB (MGBv), which is the largest subnucleus and part of the lemniscal pathway
evidence: This is established knowledge about auditory thalamus anatomy.

claim: In the mouse, calretinin (CR) is a useful marker for distinguishing between different parts of the thalamus.
source: In the mouse, calretinin (CR) has been identified as a useful marker for distinguishing between different parts of the thalamus.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Lu et al., 2009.

claim: Among the auditory subnuclei, only neurons in the MGBd, MGBm, SG, PIN and PP, but not the MGBv, contain CR.
source: Among the auditory subnuclei, only neurons in the MGBd, MGBm, SG, PIN and PP, but not the MGBv, contain CR (Lu et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The CR-IRES-cre line is suitable for targeting the non-lemniscal and paralaminar nuclei of the auditory thalamus.
source: While green labelled neurons were found throughout the auditory thalamus, red labelled neurons were found exclusively outside of the MGBv (Figure 4A,B), which confirmed that the CR-IRES-cre line is suitable for targeting the non-lemniscal and paralaminar nuclei of the auditory thalamus.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Input to the cortex from neurons in non-lemniscal and paralaminar nuclei is restricted mostly to secondary auditory areas, particularly area A2.
source: We found that input to the cortex from the neurons in these nuclei is restricted mostly to secondary auditory areas, particularly the ventrally located area A2.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The few axons from non-lemniscal and paralaminar nuclei found in primary auditory cortical areas were restricted mostly to layer 1.
source: The few axons found in primary auditory cortical areas were restricted mostly to layer 1 and the even fewer axons found in the middle layers were located primarily below the main thalamic input (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Projections from non-lemniscal and paralaminar nuclei to regions outside the auditory cortex were found mostly in the amygdala and striatum.
source: Projections to regions outside the auditory cortex were found mostly in the amygdala and striatum.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Projections from the medial part of the auditory thalamus (MGBm/PIN) provide only extremely sparse input to auditory cortex.
source: Using this approach (Chen et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2012), we were able to transfect very small numbers of neurons (12-53) and could reveal that projections from the medial part of the auditory thalamus (MGBm/PIN) provide only extremely sparse input to auditory cortex (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Input from MGBm/PIN primarily terminates in L1, and otherwise is located below the middle layer(s) where input from the MGBv is densest.
source: This input primarily terminates in L1, and otherwise is located below the middle layer(s) where input from the MGBv is densest.
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Projections from the PP do not enter the auditory cortex and instead remain subcortical where they target amygdala, striatum and midbrain.
source: Projections from the PP do not enter the auditory cortex and instead remain subcortical where they target amygdala, striatum and midbrain (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Projections from the MGBv to primary auditory cortical areas are several orders of magnitudes more extensive than the projections from other thalamic nuclei, both in L1 and in the middle layers.
source: Projections from the MGBv to primary auditory cortical areas are several orders of magnitudes more extensive than the projections from other thalamic nuclei, both in L1 and in the middle layers (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: MGBv axons tend to travel from the middle layers to L1 in columnar fashion, in an almost straight line.
source: Closer inspection of the MGBv axons revealed that they tend to travel from the middle layers to L1 in columnar fashion, that is, in an almost straight line (Figure 5C, inset)
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The columnar arrangement of MGBv axons provides an anatomical substrate for the finding that L1 and L3b/4 thalamic input are in register tonotopically and exhibit a very similar organization.
source: an arrangement which provides an anatomical substrate for our finding that L1 and L3b/4 thalamic input are in register tonotopically and exhibit a very similar organization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical observations.

claim: The arbors of MGBv axons are extraordinarily wide.
source: Furthermore, by partially reconstructing the axon from one MGBv neuron, we were able to confirm previous work in the rabbit (Cetas et al., 1999) showing how extraordinarily wide the arbors of MGBv axons tend to be
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 5D and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The same MGBv neurons provide input to different layers of the auditory cortex.
source: and that the same MGBv neurons provide input to different layers of the auditory cortex (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the anatomical data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CR+ axon boutons typically responded very poorly to acoustic stimulation.
source: These boutons typically responded very poorly to acoustic stimulation and, consequently, only very few FRAs were obtained that passed our inclusion criterion.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data from CR-IRES-cre mice.

claim: In primary auditory areas, five out of six imaged areas of CR+ axons produced no FRAs at all, and one produced three FRAs.
source: In these experiments, we first identified A2 by its ventral location and the particularly dense thalamocortical axon labelling. Areas slightly dorsal of A2 were deemed to be in primary auditory areas. Five out of six imaged areas in primary auditory areas produced no FRAs at all, and one produced three FRAs.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the experimental data.

claim: In A2, the median number of FRAs obtained per imaged area of CR+ axons was 1 ± 3.5 (range: 0–9, n = 9 areas).
source: Even in A2, where the labelling was typically very dense (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), these numbers were very low. Here, the median number of FRAs obtained per imaged area was 1 ± 3.5 (range: 0–9, n = 9 areas)
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the experimental data.

claim: Axon boutons with clearly defined FRAs are predominantly a feature of the projection from MGBv to the primary auditory cortical areas.
source: suggesting that axon boutons with clearly defined FRAs are predominantly a feature of the projection from MGBv to the primary auditory cortical areas.
evidence: This is inferred from the poor responses of CR+ axons compared to the robust responses observed in the main experiments.

claim: Auditory cortical layers 1 and 3b/4 receive tonotopically matching thalamic input.
source: We have shown that while auditory cortical layers 1 and 3b/4 receive tonotopically matching thalamic input, the frequency selectivity of neighboring axon boutons is highly heterogeneous.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The frequency selectivity of neighboring axon boutons in auditory cortical layers 1 and 3b/4 is highly heterogeneous.
source: We have shown that while auditory cortical layers 1 and 3b/4 receive tonotopically matching thalamic input, the frequency selectivity of neighboring axon boutons is highly heterogeneous.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Until recently, it has not been possible to characterize the receptive fields of individual thalamic boutons.
source: That the thalamocortical projection is topographically arranged has been known for a long time (Clark, 1936; Walker, 1937). Until recently, however, it has not been possible to characterize the receptive fields of individual thalamic boutons (Roth et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: Very similar patterns of results were observed across two strains of C57BL/6 mice and across both anesthetized and awake animals.
